\section[gotear]{gotear — to drip, to leak}

\label{lesson:ES-C769-gotear}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to beat, then the Spanish for the ingredient.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: gotear}
\textbf{gotear} — \textquotedblleft{}to drip, to leak\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El grifo goteó toda la noche.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The tap dripped all night.}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{gotear} is built on \emph{gota} 'a drop' with the ending \emph{-ear}. \emph{Gota} is inherited from Latin \emph{gutta} 'a drop' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{gotear}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{gotear}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to beat, then the Spanish for the ingredient, then say \emph{gotear} again
\end{itemize}

\section[la gotera]{la gotera — the leak (in a roof)}

\label{lesson:ES-C769-gotera}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the ingredient, then the Spanish for to drip.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la gotera}
\textbf{la gotera} — \textquotedblleft{}the leak (in a roof)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Con la lluvia salió una gotera en el techo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{With the rain a leak appeared in the ceiling.}
\end{quote}

Used for water coming through a roof or ceiling; a leaking pipe is \emph{una fuga}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{gotera} is built on \emph{gota} 'a drop' (EtymDB), which comes from Latin \emph{gutta} 'a drop', with the ending \emph{-era}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la gotera}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la gotera}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la gotera}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the ingredient, then the Spanish for to drip, then say \emph{la gotera} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la gotera mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The leak (in a roof)\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[averiado]{averiado — broken down, out of order}

\label{lesson:ES-C769-averiado}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to drip, then the Spanish for the leak.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: averiado}
\textbf{averiado} — \textquotedblleft{}broken down, out of order\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El ascensor está averiado desde el lunes.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The lift has been out of order since Monday.}
\end{quote}

For machines, with \emph{estar}. \emph{Una avería} is a breakdown.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{averiado} is built on \emph{avería} 'a breakdown, damage'. \emph{Avería} is usually traced to Arabic \emph{ʿawāriyya} 'damaged goods', through Catalan or Italian \emph{avaria}, a word of sailors and merchants.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{averiado}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{averiado}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{averiado}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to drip, then the Spanish for the leak, then say \emph{averiado} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does averiado mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Broken down, out of order\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[el fontanero]{el fontanero — the plumber}

\label{lesson:ES-C769-fontanero}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the leak, then the Spanish for broken down.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el fontanero}
\textbf{el fontanero} — \textquotedblleft{}the plumber\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
El fontanero arregló la tubería en una hora.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The plumber fixed the pipe in an hour.}
\end{quote}

This is the word in Spain; in Latin America people say \emph{el plomero}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{fontanero} is built on old \emph{fontana} 'a fountain', from Late Latin \emph{fontāna} (EtymDB), from \emph{fōns} 'a spring', with the ending \emph{-ero}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el fontanero}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el fontanero}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el fontanero}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the leak, then the Spanish for broken down, then say \emph{el fontanero} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does el fontanero mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The plumber\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[el electricista]{el electricista — the electrician}

\label{lesson:ES-C769-electricista}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for broken down, then the Spanish for the plumber.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el electricista}
\textbf{el electricista} — \textquotedblleft{}the electrician\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Llamamos a un electricista porque no había luz.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{We called an electrician because there was no power.}
\end{quote}

The same form for a woman: \emph{la electricista}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{electricista} is built on \emph{eléctrico} with the ending \emph{-ista}. \emph{Eléctrico} goes back to Greek \emph{\'{\={e}}lektron} 'amber' (Lewis \& Short, under \emph{electrum}), because rubbed amber pulls in light things.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{el electricista}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{el electricista}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for broken down, then the Spanish for the plumber, then say \emph{el electricista} again
